commit.message:
feat: put the mark beside the wordmark

The favicon was already the two panels with the midpoint between them, but
the header showed the name alone. Same drawing now sits to its left, drawn
from the tokens rather than repeated as hex so a change to the semantic pair
reaches it.

Hidden from assistive technology: the wordmark next to it already says
"Midpoint".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: drop the "the problem" kicker

The headline already reads as a problem. "Announces itself before it
executes" is self-evidently bad news, so a label above it saying so was
doing work the sentence had already done, in the register of a marketing
page rather than of a fact. The hero leads with the headline instead.

That took the last user of --accent-text with it, so the token goes too,
following --accent-strong for the same reason. --accent now marks exactly two
things, the sell side and the losing figure in the MEV panel, both of which
are genuinely adverse. That is the whole justification for the colour.

Both removed values and their measurements are kept in design.md section 2.3.
They are easy to need again and not the kind of thing to reinvent by eye:
white on --accent is 3.99:1 and fails AA for button text, and --accent itself
is too dark to read as running copy.

feat: lift the type in the cost-of-being-observed panel

Every small size in the MEV panel goes up a step: the heading 12 to 13, the
row labels and the explanation 13 to 15, the caveat 12 to 13. Padding and
margins move to tokens at the same time rather than staying as loose pixels.

One real fix fell out of it. The caveat was dimmed with `opacity: 0.75` over
--text-muted, which composites against whatever is behind and put its actual
contrast below both text tokens, so the contrast table in design.md was not
true of it. It now uses --text-faint directly and measures 4.77:1 on the
glass. design.md section 2.4 gains a rule against dimming text with opacity,
because the whole point of the token table is that it can be trusted.

feat: rebuild the footer, quiet the secondary buttons, lift note size

Four changes.

The footer was a stripe of blue monospace links over a wall of small print.
It is now two columns of equal weight: the deployed contracts as a labelled
list, so names and hashes line up rather than running together, and the
attestation disclosure beside them with a heading of its own. The disclosure
reads better as a peer of the addresses than as a footnote under them. Added
the comparison pool address while there, since the hero's fine print refers
to it and there was nowhere to look it up.

The footer also joins the lattice as its last row instead of floating below
it in a separate container.

Notes go from 13px to 15px. Thirteen is small for what is often the only
explanation on screen.

The control under "clear the batch" gets a wider gap above it, so it reads as
a separate step rather than as the next line of the paragraph.

Connect wallet keeps the specular treatment and everything else moves to
.btn-quiet, an almost-transparent grey on a hairline border. Three specular
buttons competed, and the one that actually matters to a first-time visitor
was the one that got lost. That also drops the page from four WebGL contexts
to two, and design.md now treats two as the ceiling.

feat: specular buttons in place of the crimson fills

Replaces all three primary actions (connect wallet, seal and submit, close
and settle) with SpecularButton from the registry:

  npx shadcn@latest add @react-bits/SpecularButton-TS-CSS

TS-CSS rather than the JS-CSS variant given, for the same reason as the other
two: tsc -b runs in the build and a .jsx file would need allowJs for no
benefit. Same component either way. Settings are the ones supplied, held in
PrimaryButton.tsx so the vendored file stays untouched.

Two consequences worth stating.

Each instance runs its own WebGL context and frame loop, so the page now has
four counting the aurora. Well inside the browser limit, but not free, so
PrimaryButton drops both the idle animation and the pointer tracking under
prefers-reduced-motion. design.md now treats four as the ceiling.

--accent-strong is gone. It existed only because white on --accent measures
3.99:1 and fails AA for button text, and nothing is filled with crimson any
more. The measurement is kept in design.md so the trap is not walked into
again if a crimson fill returns.

One documented deviation from the never-edit-vendored rule: SpecularButton
derives a `steer` boolean that implies `pointerAngle != null`, but the
narrowing does not survive the intermediate variable under `strict`, so
`tsc -b` failed on it. The check is repeated inline, which is a no-op at
runtime, marked in the file and recorded in design.md section 6. Re-running
`shadcn add` overwrites it and the build breaks until it is reapplied.

Bundle 171 kB gzipped against the 200 kB ceiling.

feat: the hero ends by fading, not by being cut

Removes the rounded corners from the hero band. There is now no boundary at
all: both the band's tint and the aurora above it return to transparent
before the band ends, so there is no edge and therefore no corner to shape.

The curve solved the same problem the other way round, by giving the cut a
shape rather than removing it. Fading removes it.

Both halves have to fade or neither works. The aurora mask now has a long
tail at the bottom, because a short one reads as a gradient band, which is a
softer boundary rather than no boundary. And the band's own tint fades with
it; leaving that opaque would draw the exact line the fade exists to remove.

--radius-band is gone rather than left unused.

feat: dotted full-bleed lattice, no fills behind the content

Reworks the ruled sheet into what was actually asked for. The previous version
still drew a box: a bordered rectangle with a background, ruled inside. This
draws lines instead.

Three properties carry it, and losing any one turns it back into boxes:

- The rules are full bleed. Rows span the viewport so their horizontal lines
  run edge to edge rather than stopping at the content column, and the two
  outer verticals span the whole lattice so they read as one continuous rule
  passing behind everything.
- Nothing has a fill. No cell has a background. A ruled sheet with a
  background is still a box.
- Dotted rather than solid, since solid hairlines at this density read as a
  table.

The row containers drop their horizontal padding so a cell's edge lands
exactly on the vertical rule, with the cell's own padding providing the gap.
--rule lifts from #232935 to #333c4d, because dots carry roughly half the ink
of a solid line and disappeared at the old value.

The sheen ends up on the glass MEV card alone. It began on six cards, moved to
the sheet, and has now run out of edges to catch light on, which is fine: one
lit surface on a page is the right number.

feat: rule the content into one sheet, and fix form control fonts

Two fixes.

Buttons were rendering in the browser's default face while the rest of the
page was in Inter. Form controls do not inherit typography from their
ancestors, so setting a face on body leaves every button, input, select and
textarea behind. `font: inherit` spells it out. Inputs keep the mono face,
which is deliberate: they hold numbers.

The six bordered rounded rectangles are gone. Content is now divided by ruled
lines: one sheet with a hairline border, ruled internally into cells, over a
faint square lattice at about 4% alpha. Six boxes read as six unrelated
widgets sharing a page; a ruled sheet reads as one instrument, which is what
this is.

The rules are drawn by the cells themselves rather than by a gap-and-
background trick, so every line is continuous and lands on an exact pixel.
Below 820px the columns collapse and the vertical rule becomes a horizontal
one, since a vertical rule with nothing beside it is a stray mark.

Two things moved rather than being dropped. The sheen now sits on the sheet:
one lit rectangle instead of six. And the public/private colours became
legend swatches beside the two headings, because there are no card borders
left to colour and design.md section 2.1 does not allow that signal to
weaken just because the layout changed.

Renamed the new row class to .sheet-row after finding it collided with the
existing .row used for input groups.

feat: remove the decorative pills from the hero and header

Drops the "Live on Flare Coston2" badge and the "Coston2" chip. Both said
the same thing as each other and as the tagline, which already ends "settled
on Coston2", so the page announced its network three times before saying
anything about the product.

The hero now opens straight on the kicker and the headline.

The enclave and account chips stay. Those are not decoration: they report
which enclave is answering and which account is connected, and they only
appear once there is something to report.

Also removes the now-unused .badge and .badge-dot rules rather than leaving
them to rot.

fix: declare color-scheme dark, so the glass is actually visible

The pills rendered as flat dark blobs with no glass at all. The cause was
nowhere near the symptom: GlassSurface paints its rim highlights through
light-dark(), and a page with no color-scheme declared defaults to light no
matter how dark its own colours are. The highlights were resolving to black
on a black page.

One declaration on :root fixes it, rather than tuning the component's
numbers, which is where I would have gone looking next. It also fixes native
scrollbars and form controls, which had been light-themed on a dark page.

Rim highlights now resolve to white at 35%, and pill contrast improves as a
side effect: 7.6:1 on the badge and 6.7:1 on the chips, up from 6.9 and 6.4.

Recorded in design.md section 6, including the limitation worth being plain
about: on a flat near-black backdrop there is nothing behind a pill to
refract, so what reads as glass is the frost and the rim light. The
distortion only shows where something sits behind it.

feat: border sheen on panels, glass pills for chips and badge

Panels now carry a hairline lit at two opposite corners, matching the
reference. Measured rather than eyeballed: brightest at top-right, order
TR > BR > BL > TL, 1.60x bright:dim against the reference's 1.66x.

The part that makes it read as light rather than as a glowing outline is that
only two corners are lit. On a 45 degree axis the other two sit at the
midpoint of the gradient and stay dark. Lighting all four is the usual way
this effect ends up looking cheap.

Built as a masked pseudo-element, not the usual two-background
background-clip recipe, because that recipe has to paint a background and
would destroy the backdrop-filter on the glass card. Painting only the ring
means one rule serves both solid and glass surfaces. The element keeps its
ordinary border, so the gradient only adds highlights and the edge never
vanishes where the gradient is transparent.

The public and private panels are clipped clear of their left edge. That
coloured border is the semantic signal design.md section 2.1 exists to
protect, and a neutral highlight must not compete with it.

Chips and the hero badge move onto GlassSurface, also installed through the
registry:

  npx shadcn@latest add @react-bits/GlassSurface-TS-CSS

Three of its defaults are overridden in GlassPill.tsx, and the first is not
optional: mixBlendMode ships as difference, which inverts what is behind it
and turns a subtle pill into a bright inverted patch on a near-black page.
width and height ship as fixed pixels, so both are handed to CSS instead,
because a pill has to size to its label. The vendored file is untouched.

Pill text measures 6.9:1 on the badge and 6.4:1 on the chips, so the glass
costs no legibility. Bundle 169 kB gzipped against the 200 kB ceiling.

feat: curved hero, shadcn registry, softer aurora

Three changes.

The hero band's bottom corners are now rounded and the band clips its
contents, so the aurora ends on a curve rather than a straight line. The clip
is the shape: the glow runs bright all the way to the boundary and the radius
cuts it. The previous version faded the glow out before the edge, which
avoided the hard line but left nothing to curve. The band also carries a faint
tint of its own, because a rounded corner between two identical near-blacks is
invisible.

Aurora now installs through the shadcn CLI rather than being pasted:

  npx shadcn@latest add @react-bits/Aurora-TS-CSS

TS-CSS rather than JS-CSS, since tsc -b runs in the build and a .jsx file
would need allowJs for no benefit; the two variants are the same component.
The vendored file is byte-for-byte upstream and never edited, so re-running
add is safe and upstream fixes arrive as a clean diff. Reduced-motion and
tab-visibility handling moved out into AuroraBackdrop.tsx, which controls
whether the component is mounted at all rather than patching its render loop.
Unmounting also releases the WebGL context outright instead of leaving it
alive on a throttled loop.

blend drops from 0.5 to 0.28. The wide default smoothstep spread the band into
an even wash, and the shape of the light is the point.

Not adopted, and design.md section 6 says why: shadcn's token names, because
--public and --private carry an argument that --primary and --secondary
cannot, and Tailwind, because every registry item used here is a -CSS variant
that ships plain CSS.

Bundle 167 kB gzipped, unchanged, against the 200 kB ceiling.

feat: React Bits Aurora, full bleed behind the hero

Replaces the CSS approximation with the real component from reactbits.dev
(MIT), ported from the upstream JSX to TypeScript. Simplex noise drives a
height field ramped through three colour stops, rendered through OGL. The
shader is verbatim so it stays comparable with upstream.

The CSS version was wrong and looked it: blurred radial gradients read as a
flat blue rectangle rather than as light. The noise field is what makes the
effect look like anything, and there is no cheap way to fake it.

Also fixes the page being boxed in. The content column was 1080px, so a wide
display showed a narrow strip with dead space either side. The hero is now
full bleed, with `.hero-band` spanning the viewport and carrying the canvas
while `.hero` stays contained, and the container is 1200px.

Three things the port needed beyond a straight copy:

- The canvas is flipped. The shader's intensity rises with uv.y and uv.y is 0
  at the bottom in GL coordinates, so upstream draws its band at the top. The
  reference has light rising from below. Flipping the canvas rather than
  editing the shader keeps the shader comparable.
- The mask fades in at the top and back out at the bottom. Without the second
  fade the glow is still at full strength where the band clips it, which drew
  a hard horizontal line across the page.
- Colour stops are read from the --aurora-* tokens at mount rather than
  repeated in the component, so the tokens stay the single source of truth.

Two additions upstream does not have: the loop never starts under
prefers-reduced-motion (one static frame is drawn instead), and it is
cancelled outright when the tab is hidden rather than left to the browser to
throttle.

design.md section 5.3 and the performance budget are rewritten to match. The
earlier version argued for CSS over React Bits, which is no longer the
decision, and claimed zero running canvases, which is no longer true. Bundle
is 167 kB gzipped against a 200 kB ceiling.

feat: design system, tokens, and an aurora behind the hero

design.md documents the system; web/src/styles/tokens.css holds the values.
The hero follows the reference brief: pill badge, large headline at regular
weight, muted body, a stat row, and a glass card, with two deliberate
departures. No white fade at the bottom, and blue rather than purple.

Type is Outfit for display and Inter for the rest, self-hosted through
@fontsource so the page makes no external font request. Latin subset only,
which took the font payload from 280K to 96K.

The aurora is CSS rather than React Bits. Its Aurora pulls in OGL and runs a
WebGL context and a fragment shader every frame for as long as the page is
open, and this is an interface people leave sitting in a tab. Three blurred
blobs drifting on mutually prime periods get close enough, animate only
transform so the work stays on the compositor, and stop dead under
prefers-reduced-motion.

Three bugs found and fixed while building it, all recorded in design.md so
they are not reintroduced:

- The aurora painted over the copy. The hero columns were statically
  positioned, so they did not participate in z-ordering against a positioned
  sibling. This looked exactly like a contrast problem and was not one.
- The clip drew a visible rectangle where the glow was still bright at the
  hero boundary. The mask now fades on every side.
- The oversized blob box widened the page into a horizontal scrollbar.

Two genuine accessibility failures found by measuring rather than eyeballing:
--text-faint was 4.06:1 and is now 5.4:1, and white on --accent is 3.99:1,
which is why button fills use --accent-strong at 5.09:1. Body text also lifts
from 15px to 16px under 820px.

The blue tension is handled rather than ignored: --public is already the
colour of "what the chain sees", so the aurora ramp sits deeper and more
saturated, ambient only, and never appears outside the hero.

feat: lead the page with the problem, priced from the live pool

A visitor arriving cold met a disabled deposit form and a one-sentence
tagline. Nothing told them what the venue is for, and the strongest evidence
this project has, the measured cost of trading in the open, existed only in
a terminal script.

The page now opens with the problem, then prices it, then shows the
public/private contrast, and only then the controls. Same URL, same app,
different order.

The figure is computed from the comparison pool's live reserves rather than
recorded, so it cannot go stale. sandwich.ts reproduces NaiveAmm.quoteOut
including its integer truncation, and agrees with the verified live run to
the last digit on prices (1.048538 unobserved, 1.133141 sandwiched); the
one-bp difference in the headline is the script rounding where this
truncates.

Degrades in the right direction: the estimate needs only the public RPC, so
the argument still stands when the enclave is offline, and falls back to the
recorded 746 bps if even the pool is unreachable.

Also finally untracks web/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo. The earlier attempt staged it
with `git add -u` straight after removing it, which put it back.
chore: untrack playwright scratch output

docs: screenshot of the live site

Taken from https://major101x.github.io/midpoint/ rather than localhost, so
it is evidence the hosted build works: the enclave chip only renders if the
cross-origin fetch to the proxy succeeded.

feat: favicon, and document the hosted build

The favicon is inlined as a data URI rather than served from public/,
because a file reference would have to carry the Pages base path and this
does not. It was also the last console error on the live page.

Records the hosting setup in web/README.md and day 13 in the build log,
including the limitation worth being upfront about: the link is only fully
live while the enclave stack and tunnel are running, since in FCC
development mode the enclave is on the operator's machine.

style: forge fmt NaiveAmm

Three signatures were over the line limit, which CI checks with
forge fmt --check. Caught by the first run against the new remote.

feat: make the web build hostable, so there is a live link

The page could only ever run on the machine that built it. It calls the FCC
proxy through `/tee`, which exists solely as a Vite dev-server forwarder;
a production build is three static files with nothing standing behind them,
so every one of those calls would have 404'd on a host.

Three things were needed:

- A configurable proxy base. VITE_TEE_URL at build time, falling back to
  `/tee` so local development is unchanged.
- CORS. The proxy sends no CORS headers, and the page's ngrok-skip header
  makes requests non-simple, so a preflight goes out first and the proxy
  would answer it with a bare 404. web/ngrok-policy.yml answers the
  preflight at the tunnel and adds the header to everything else. The
  allow-origin header is set in exactly one of the two rules, since a
  duplicate is a CORS failure rather than a harmless repeat.
- A base path. GitHub Pages serves a project site from /<repo>/, and
  without the prefix every asset 404s.

Publishing the proxy exposes nothing new: post-build.sh already registers
that same URL on chain as the extension's proxy endpoint, and the endpoints
the page touches return either public chain data or a signed result meant
to be relayed on chain.

The page now degrades honestly. On-chain state still renders when the
enclave is offline, since that comes from the public RPC; only sealing a new
order needs the proxy, and the error says so.

docs: stop recording Flare's indexer host

The host address was shared privately in Telegram and belongs to Flare, not
to this project. It does not need to be in a repository that is about to be
public. The credentials were never recorded here; both now live only in the
gitignored proxy config.

chore: actually stop tracking build artifacts

The earlier attempt at this did not hold. forge init writes `!/broadcast`
into contracts/.gitignore, which negates the `broadcast/` rule in the root
.gitignore, so the files came straight back on the next `git add -A` and
grew from three to six. Removing the negation is the actual fix.

Same treatment for web/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo, which is incremental compiler
state and was never meant to be committed.

chore: rename the venue to Midpoint

A dark pool crosses at the midpoint of the spread, and this venue's auction
clears at the midpoint of the tied price range. The word carries both halves
of what this is.

Scope is deliberately the product name only. The on-chain op-type constant
stays bytes32("SEALED"): it is deployed in the live OrderBook and matched by
the extension's handler registration, so changing it would cost a redeploy,
a re-registration and a new extension id for no gain. "Sealed-bid" is also
still the correct name for the mechanism.

Left "Sealed in the browser" in App.tsx alone, since that one is the verb.

Fixed the architecture diagram's box alignment while editing it. The
interior lines were already 1 to 2 characters wider than the border.

log: day 12, the MEV claim measured instead of asserted

746 bps extracted on the public pool, 0 in the venue, stable across five
runs. Records the two honest limits (no public mempool on Coston2, shallow
faucet-capped pool) and the five problems hit getting there, including a
second zombie TEE machine and the FTSO band correctly rejecting a batch.

Also backfills day 11, the web interface, which shipped without a log entry.

feat: side-by-side comparison, sandwiched pool against sealed venue

Runs the same trade down both paths on Coston2 and prints what it costs to
be observed: 746 bps on the public pool, 0 in the venue. Measured live,
not asserted.

Details that took a few attempts to get right:

- Trade sizes are fractions of the reserves, not absolute amounts, because
  testnet FXRP is faucet-capped and constant-product pricing is scale
  invariant. Pool depth is printed alongside every result.
- An arbitrage step returns the pool to the FTSO price before measuring, so
  runs do not inherit the previous run's skew and the absolute prices stay
  comparable with the venue's.
- Limits on the sealed side are derived from the live feed. Hardcoded ones
  cleared at 1.074488 against a feed of 1.029415 and Settlement rejected
  the batch with PriceOutsideBand, which is the guard doing its job.
- Gas is padded 50%. FXRP is a FAssets proxy that delegates twice, and an
  under-estimate surfaces as OutOfGas inside the token rather than as
  anything legible.
- The searcher's unwind sits in a finally block, so a failure mid-sandwich
  does not leave the pool skewed for the next run.

Coston2 has no public mempool, so the script cannot race for the ordering a
real searcher races for; it executes the three transactions in the order a
successful searcher achieves. Stated in the file header rather than left
for a reader to discover.

chore: stop tracking forge broadcast artifacts

.gitignore has excluded broadcast/ since the first commit, but these three
files predate the rule and were carried along. They are build output, and
the deployed addresses that matter are recorded in PROGRESS.md and spec.md
section 3, which is where anyone should be reading them from.

feat: naive constant-product pool as the comparison baseline

NaiveAmm is the venue this project argues against: a correct x*y=k pool
with a 30 bps fee, tracked reserves and a slippage bound. Nothing in it is
deliberately broken, which is the point. Sandwich.t.sol front-runs it and
the victim still loses, because the vulnerability is in the shape of the
venue rather than in a bug a careful developer would have caught.

Nine tests, including a fuzz run over victim and attacker sizes asserting
that front-running never improves the victim's fill, and one showing that
a tight slippage bound converts the loss into a failed trade rather than
preventing the extraction.

Lives under src/demo so it cannot be mistaken for part of the venue.

feat: web interface built around the public/private contrast

Two panels side by side: what the chain sees (batch, order count, pinned
enclave, and your order as opaque ciphertext) against what only the
enclave sees (side, limit, size, unfilled orders, the resting book).
That contrast is the product, so the interface is arranged around it and
nothing else competes.

Orders are sealed in the browser with the same ECIES the client package
tests, adapted to drop Node's Buffer. Plaintext never leaves the page.

Vite proxies /tee to the FCC proxy because it sends no CORS headers.

The order form mirrors the enclave's collateral rule so an order the TEE
would reject is caught before it costs an instruction fee.

Verified against the live deployment: renders batch #2, the pinned
enclave 0x02a2Dd00, and last settled batch #1.

log: day 10, collateral guard live and verified on chain

Also makes the demo deposit what a wallet actually holds, so it survives
a redeploy stranding balances in the previous vault, and adds an
overcommit probe that shows the enclave rejecting an order the chain
cannot see.

fix: enclave rejects orders the vault cannot cover

Found by running the venue. The first live settlement reverted with
Vault.InsufficientBalance: a trader had sold four FXRP across two orders
while holding three. The enclave was clearing blind, because it cannot
read the vault.

The damage is collective, which is what makes this worth guarding rather
than leaving to chance: one trader overcommitting reverts the whole batch
and strands everyone else in it until someone voids it.

OrderBook now reads the submitter's vault balances on chain and sends
them with the order. That leaks nothing, since vault balances are already
public and anyone can read them directly.

The enclave reserves conservatively and cumulatively per trader per
batch: a sell commits its size in base, a buy commits size times its own
limit price, which is an upper bound because buyers pay the clearing
price and that is never worse than their limit. Cumulative matters:
checking orders in isolation would let five orders that each fit a
balance, and together do not, all through.

76 Solidity tests, 93 extension.
log: day 9, first sealed batch settled on Coston2

feat: relayer and end-to-end demo, first sealed batch settled

The relayer carries the enclave's signed batch result from the FCC proxy
to Settlement. Deliberately untrusted: it can delay settlement or refuse
to run, but cannot forge or alter a batch, because Settlement checks the
signature against the enclave OrderBook pinned for that batch. Anyone can
run one, and a second changes nothing since the first advances the batch.

demo.mjs runs the whole flow against Coston2: deposit, seal client side,
submit as opaque bytes, close, relay, settle. Deposits are idempotent and
it waits out the batch window rather than assuming it can close instantly.

First settled batch on Coston2:
  batch 1, clearing price 1.065000, volume 4.000000 FXRP
  tx 0xa827f1710adb808965dedbc66fa61cb7a2d13b28ba3b311f2cfeccd212bbd043
  maker  4 FXRP -> 4.26 USDT0
  taker  5 USDT0 -> 4 FXRP + 0.74 USDT0
  base and quote both conserved
log: day 8 complete, Settlement with four verification checks

feat: Settlement verifies the enclave, the oracle, and conservation

Four independent checks before any balance moves:

  1. The signature must recover to the exact TEE machine OrderBook pinned
     for this batch. Not any registered TEE, and not an admin-set address:
     the enclave that actually held the book. Nobody else can produce it,
     including the operator, and there is a test for that.
  2. Only the currently closed batch settles, and settling advances it, so
     a payload cannot be applied twice.
  3. The clearing price must sit within a band of the FTSO oracle. This is
     what bounds a hidden engine's discretion and is why the venue does
     not require blind trust in the TEE.
  4. Base bought must equal base sold and quote paid must equal quote
     received. Value can move between traders, never appear or vanish.

Quote is now allocated inside the enclave rather than derived per fill on
chain. Both sides trade the same total base, but flooring each fill
separately makes the totals diverge whenever one side has more fills than
the other, which would leave settlement short and revert the batch. The
enclave computes the total once and splits it exactly, reusing the
remainder logic already property-tested.

Includes a cross-language conformance test: a payload produced by the
real extension encoder is decoded and settled in Solidity, so the two
sides cannot drift apart silently.

74 Solidity tests, 82 extension.

fix: add voidBatch so a vanished enclave cannot strand a batch

Found on chain. TEE machines are ephemeral and old ones linger in the
registry: after two rebuilds, getActiveTeeMachines listed three machines
for our extension, two of them dead, all advertising the same URL. Two
thirds of batches were being pinned to enclaves that no longer existed.

Pausing the dead machines then exposed the real flaw. batchTee is pinned
for the batch's lifetime, so once that machine is paused, closeBatch
reverts inside the registry and advanceBatch cannot run because the batch
never closed. The batch is stuck permanently, and so is every balance
frozen behind it.

voidBatch abandons such a batch without going through the enclave. It is
deliberately permissionless with no owner shortcut: letting the operator
void immediately would let them cancel any batch whose outcome they
disliked, which is the discretion this venue exists to remove. Everyone
waits out voidDelay, including the operator.

Orders in a voided batch are never revealed and never settle; traders
keep their balances and can resubmit.

50 Solidity tests.
log: day 7 complete, uniform-price clearing with signed payloads

feat: uniform-price clearing and TEE-signed settlement payloads

Clears each batch at one price: maximise executed volume, break ties by
minimising imbalance, then take the midpoint of the tied range so the
surplus is split rather than handed to one side. Allocation respects
price priority, and orders sitting exactly at the clearing price are
rationed pro-rata, never by arrival, since rationing by arrival would
rebuild the queue race the venue exists to remove.

All arithmetic is integer. The pro-rata remainder is distributed by
largest fractional entitlement so fills sum exactly; settlement requires
both sides to net to zero, so an off-by-one would revert the batch.
Mutation-checked: removing the remainder distribution fails two tests.

Correctness is argued by property test as well as by example. 400 random
books are checked against an independent brute-force optimum, plus
conservation, no overfill, and nobody trading outside their limit.

RUN_MATCH now signs the ABI-encoded settlement payload via the sign
port's POST /sign, using the TEE identity key whose address is the
registered machine id, so no key is ever distributed or stored.

The book is consumed only after a signature exists. Deleting earlier
would let an unreachable sign port destroy a batch with no way to retry.
That has its own regression test.

feat: seal orders client-side, decrypt and validate in the enclave

Determined the encryption scheme by reading tee-node: it calls
ecies.Decrypt with go-ethereum defaults (ECIES_AES128_SHA256). The common
JavaScript ECIES libraries are not wire-compatible with that, so the
scheme is implemented directly against geth's layout:

  R(65) || IV(16) || AES-128-CTR || HMAC-SHA256(32)
  Ke/Km from the NIST SP 800-56 concat KDF over the ECDH x coordinate

Verified against the live enclave: an order sealed by client/ decrypts
inside the TEE with every field intact.

The enclave now decrypts each order and rejects it unless the trader and
batchId inside the ciphertext match the ones OrderBook took from
msg.sender. That check is what makes the duplicated fields worth their
bytes: it stops a ciphertext lifted from a public transaction being
replayed by someone else or into a later batch.

Handler errors are kept terse on purpose. They surface in action results
that anyone can read through the proxy, so a validation message must
never carry a price or size; there is a test asserting exactly that.

feat: OrderBook relays encrypted orders and pins the batch enclave

The order book lives in one enclave's memory, and getRandomTeeIds is a
view function, so its randomness comes from block state and its answer
changes between blocks. A batch spans many blocks, so drawing a machine
per order would scatter one batch across enclaves and clear against a
partial book. The machine is drawn once, on the batch's first order.

msg.sender and the batch id are ABI-encoded alongside the ciphertext so
the enclave can reject a replayed blob rather than trusting the trader
field inside the encrypted payload.

closeBatch is permissionless so liveness does not depend on the operator,
but rate limited so nobody can isolate a single order into its own batch
and read its side off the settlement.

feat: Vault holds trader balances so order sizes stay private

Per-order escrow would publish the order size on chain and make the order
encryption decorative. Traders instead pre-fund an internal balance and
draw orders against it, decoupling the public deposit from the private
order in both time and amount.

Because the chain cannot see an encrypted order's size, it cannot lock
the right amount at submission. Withdrawals are frozen for the duration
of a settling batch instead.

SafeTransfer tolerates tokens that omit the bool return, which the USDT
lineage does. Deposits credit the amount actually received, so a
fee-on-transfer token cannot leave the vault insolvent.

spec: resolve Q1, settlement signs with an in-enclave key

Investigated reusing the TEE's native result signature and rejected it.
The identity key does equal the registered machine id, but the documented
signing construction could not be reproduced, and a control test against
the proxy signature with its known private key failed too. No on-chain
verification helper exists in VerificationFacet.

Settlement will instead use the documented fce-sign pattern: an in-enclave
secp256k1 key producing 65-byte r||s||v, verified with ecrecover.

Also records that TEE keys are ephemeral across container restarts, so the
signer address must be mutable storage, never a constant.
